blocks.title: The surface changes in the bend
blocks.content: A rider sees packed gravel at the start of a bend and loose stones farther through it. The corner still looks wide. The temptation is to carry the same speed and fix the line later. A better choice is to slow while the bike is mostly upright and choose a path with a clear exit. The loose patch may shift under the tires; no speed printed in a lesson can tell you how much grip will be there.

blocks.label: Weight through the outside foot, eyes through the exit
blocks.content: Start with a wide, low-speed turn in an empty gravel area. Keep your inside pedal clear of the ground and feel your weight through the outside foot. Let the bike lean under you while your torso stays comfortably upright. Keep both hands on the bars with a light, secure grip and look where you want to go. If you need to force the bike around, make the turn wider or ride slower.

### Pick the line you can see

Look for an open exit and a surface that stays consistent through the bend. A smooth, wide line may be easier to ride than the shortest one. Avoid crossing loose patches, ruts, or wet pavement markings while the bike is heavily leaned if a safer path is available. Leave room for people and traffic; never use the opposite lane or a blind exit to make a corner feel easier.

Choose a speed you can manage before turning. Brake smoothly with both brakes on the straighter approach when you can. As the bike leans, ease heavy brake pressure and steer without a sudden correction. If you still need to slow, make the input gentle and give yourself more room.

items.title: Outside foot and bike lean
items.content: On a loose, flat turn, dropping and weighting the outside pedal can help you keep the inside pedal clear and support the bike as it leans beneath you. Stay balanced over the bike rather than hanging off the bars. The exact position changes with the turn, surface, bike, and rider. Practice the movement slowly on a wide bend before trying it on a trail. British Cycling’s gravel guidance describes keeping the body more upright while leaning the bike on loose off-road surfaces.

blocks.content: Use the hand position that lets you brake and steer securely on your bike. If you move to the drops for a descent, practice that position on easy ground first. Keep a firm hold on the bars without locking your elbows.

### When grip is uncertain

Slow earlier, leave a wider line, and keep more space between riders. Wet clay, loose stones over hardpack, sand, and hidden ruts can feel different within the same bend. If you cannot see the exit or a safe runout, treat the corner as unknown and enter slowly enough to stop within the visible space.

A front tire that begins to push is a sign that the current speed, line, and surface are not working together. Do not use that feeling as a target for practice. Reset on a wider, slower line, or stop the session if the surface is unpredictable.

blocks.title: The Corner Check
blocks.description: A repeatable sequence for a visible bend. It is a set of observations, not a calculated speed limit.

steps.detail: Find the exit, traffic, and any change in surface. Leave enough room to stop within what you can see.
Favor a consistent surface and a clear runout over a short or fast line.
Use both brakes smoothly while mostly upright, early enough that turning does not feel rushed.
Keep the inside pedal clear, weight the outside foot comfortably, and look toward the exit.
If grip or visibility changes, reduce abrupt inputs and allow a wider, slower path when it is safe.

blocks.title: Wide Figure-8 Practice
blocks.description: Use two markers in a flat, traffic-free area with a clear runout. Make the turns wide enough to stay comfortable; the goal is a repeatable line, not finding the point where a tire slides.

variants.label: Walking-pace turns
steps: Place two visible markers far enough apart for broad turns. Check for holes, loose debris, people, and traffic.
Ride a wide figure-eight at a pace that lets you stop easily. Look through each turn and keep the inside pedal clear.
Notice the outside-foot support and whether your hands stay light but secure.
Repeat only while the line feels calm. Widen the turns or stop if the tires push or the surface changes.

variants.label: Compare two safe lines
steps: On the same open area, try a second line that stays on a different but predictable patch of gravel.
Keep the same comfortable pace. Note how sightline and surface change the amount of steering you need.
Return to the line that gives you more room and clearer feedback. Do not increase speed to force a comparison.

proof_gate.description: You can repeat a broad turn in both directions while looking through the exit and keeping the bike under control.
proof_gate.target: Consistent line at a comfortable speed, without a tire slide or speed target

blocks.title: If the corner stops feeling predictable

scenarios.label: A tire begins to push
scenarios.situation: The bike drifts wider than your chosen line.
steps: Look toward the open, rideable space and avoid a sudden steering or braking grab.
Let the line widen if there is safe room; reduce your demands on the tires.
After stopping safely, choose a slower entry or end the drill.

blocks.content:
### Keep a cornering note

On a familiar, visible practice corner, record the surface, weather, sightline, line choice, and where you began slowing. Use the note to compare what changed between rides. Do not turn a calculated corner speed into a target on an unfamiliar road.

blocks.title: OVER 40 MOUNTAIN BIKE TIPS: CORNERING WITH CONFIDENCE | Loose over Hardpack!
blocks.caption: Cornering specifically on loose-over-hardpack — Dirt Craft's exact surface.

blocks.question: A gravel bend has loose stones halfway through and you can see the exit. What should you decide on the approach?

options.text: Choose a clear line and slow while the bike is mostly upright
Use a calculated maximum speed for that surface
Wait for the loose stones and brake hard while leaned over
Use the opposite lane to keep the turn wide

blocks.explanation: Set a manageable speed before the bend and keep the line within the space you can see and use. Loose stones can move, so a fixed speed is not a safety guarantee.

blocks.content: Before the next lesson, practice wide, low-speed figure-eights in an empty area. Note one line that gave you a clear view through the exit. Stop before the tires begin to slide.
In Climbing Without Spinning Out, you will use the same calm inputs on a loose climb and test gearing on the bike rather than trusting a calculated result.
